Swear
SWAIR
v.
Old English swerian, “to swear, take an oath.” Renders the Hebrew shāba, “to swear,” literally “to seven oneself” (oath-taking by sevens), and the Greek omnuō, “to swear, take an oath.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To swear, in Scripture, is to take an oath—to invoke God’s name and witness in confirmation of one’s word, binding oneself under the most awful sanction to the truth of what is sworn or the performance of what is promised. Oath-taking is biblical: God Himself swears (by myself have I sworn, saith the LORD); He confirms His promise to Abraham with an oath (that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation); the patriarchs swear; the magistrates swear; witnesses swear in formal proceedings; and the New Testament shows the apostles using solemn oath-language (God is my witness; before God, I lie not). Christ’s teaching on swearing in the Sermon on the Mount—swear not at all... but let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay; for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil—has been read by some traditions (Anabaptist, Quaker) as a categorical prohibition of all oath-taking; the historic Reformed and Lutheran churches have read it as a prohibition of the casual, evasive, manipulative oath-swearing of the surrounding culture, not as the abolition of lawful and solemn oaths before magistrates and in formal civil and ecclesial life—a reading reinforced by Christ’s own answer under adjuration in Matthew 26 and the apostles’ solemn oath-language across the epistles. The biblical regulation of swearing is therefore threefold. What may be sworn: only what is true and what one will perform. By whom one may swear: only by God—not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, the temple, or one’s own head, all of which Christ explicitly forbids as substitutes for swearing by God Himself. And when one should swear: rarely, weightily, only when the matter calls for the solemn confirmation an oath supplies—and never in the casual, profane, or manipulative register of ordinary speech, where the third commandment’s severity is most often broken by those who imagine themselves religious.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SWEAR as to affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed; to make a solemn promise with an appeal to God for sincerity.

expand to see more

SWEAR, v.i. — 1. To affirm or utter a solemn declaration, with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed. 2. To promise upon oath. 3. To give evidence on oath; as, to swear to the truth of a statement. 4. To use the name of God or any sacred thing in vain or profanely; as, to swear vainly, to swear profanely.

SWEAR, v.t. — 1. To utter, with an appeal to God or to some sacred object; as, to swear an oath. 2. To put to an oath; to cause to take an oath; as, to swear witnesses.

📖 Key Scripture

Hebrews 6:13-14 — "For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself, Saying, Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee."

Hebrews 6:17-18 — "Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation..."

Matthew 5:34-37 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne... But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

James 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Swearing is corrupted, on one side, by the casual profanity that drops God’s name and Christ’s name into ordinary speech as filler or expletive in plain violation of the third commandment—and on the other by the Anabaptist-style absolute prohibition that misreads Matthew 5 against the explicit biblical pattern of God’s own oaths and the apostles’ solemn oath-language.

expand to see more

The pervasive contemporary corruption of swearing is the casual profanity that has saturated ordinary speech: God’s name, Christ’s name, and the related sacred terms are dropped into ordinary speech as exclamation, filler, or expletive at a rate that earlier Christian centuries would have found shocking, and that the third commandment’s severity (the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain) plainly forbids. Believers absorb the surrounding register often unconsciously and bring it even into prayer and worship without recognizing the violation. Recover the third commandment’s gravity, and ordinary speech is purged of the profane uses that, more than any other corruption, demonstrate the shrunken doctrine of God in the contemporary church. The cleansing of speech is in this sense the most testable mark of a recovered fear of the LORD.

The opposite corruption is the Anabaptist-style absolute prohibition that reads Christ’s swear not at all as forbidding every oath in every circumstance, including solemn judicial oaths before magistrates and formal ecclesiastical oaths. The historic Reformed and Lutheran churches have rejected this reading on the explicit evidence of the biblical text: God Himself swears (Heb 6:13-18); Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and the prophets swear; Christ answers under formal adjuration in Matthew 26; Paul uses solemn oath-language repeatedly (Rom 1:9; 2 Cor 1:23; Gal 1:20; Phil 1:8; 1 Thess 2:5, 10). What Christ forbids in the Sermon on the Mount is the casual, evasive, manipulative oath-swearing of the surrounding culture—swearing by heaven or by the temple to escape the obligations of swearing by God, and the inflation of ordinary speech with oaths to compensate for habitual untruthfulness. The biblical regulation stands: only by God, only what is true, only when the matter genuinely calls for the solemn confirmation of an oath—and never in the casual or profane register that the contemporary corruption has normalized.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shāba (to swear, literally “to seven oneself”) and Greek omnuō (to swear, take an oath)—the solemn invocation of God’s name in confirmation, regulated by the third commandment and Christ’s warnings against casual and evasive oaths.

expand to see more

Hebrew shāba (H7650) — to swear, take an oath (literally “to seven oneself”).

Hebrew shābū‘āh (H7621) — oath, sworn covenant (the noun).

Greek omnuō (G3660) — to swear, take an oath.

Greek horkos (G3727) — an oath (the noun).

Usage

"God Himself swears—by myself have I sworn—and confirms His promise to Abraham with an oath as a strong consolation to the heirs of promise."

"Christ forbids the casual, evasive, manipulative oath-swearing of the surrounding culture, not the lawful and solemn oath confessed by every Reformed and Lutheran tradition."

"Casual profanity that drops God’s name into ordinary speech as filler is the most pervasive contemporary violation of the third commandment’s severity."
